messages.subject: Inference for log-Gaussian Cox processes
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm writing a master's thesis about "Interaction Modelling of inhomogeneous Poisson processes by means of log-Gaussian Cox processes". At the moment I'm in the one-dimensional case and I use the formula 2.4 on page 1504 of A TOOLBOX FOR FITTING COMPLEX SPATIAL POINT PROCESS MODELS USING INTEGRATED NESTED LAPLACE APPROXIMATION (INLA) by Illian et al. (2012) (without the constructed covariate and with only one spatially structured effect) for the simulation of a Poisson process. For the variance of the spatially UNSTRUCTURED effect (nugget effect) I use the value 0.1 (but the exact value doesn't matter, the following problem stays the same for other values not equal to 0).

My problem is as follows: If I simulate a Poisson process based on this latent process eta_{ij} and I want to regain the parameters of the formula by:

Z ~ 1 + f(i, model=spde1) + f(j, model="iid"),

I always get a precision parameter for j which is equivalent to virtual no variance (precisions of 10^5). That is, if I do inference based on the Poisson process (I have a grid based approach with counts in the grid cells), the nugget effect isn't recognized. Instead, the mean of the latent process is estimated slightly higher -- that is false -- than without a nugget effect.
In contrast, if I simulate only the latent process and estimate it with INLA, the nugget effect IS recognized.

So my question is: Can't INLA recognize nugget effects of the latent field if one wants to make inference for a log-Gauss Cox process? Perhaps because INLA "puts" this effect to the randomness of the overlying Poisson process? This would also explain why in your "The R-INLA tutorial on SPDE models" (Chapter 13 and following) log-Cox processes are always simulated without any nugget effect.

Thank you for your advice!

Best regards,
      Oliver

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Inference for log-Gaussian Cox processes
messages.body_plain:
The intensity in a log-Gaussian Cox point process has to be integrable. A "nugget effect" is not integrable, so it doesn't make sense to have that in a continuous domain model. One would have to have some spatial correlation for it to make sense, but then it wouldn't strictly be a nugget effect anymore.

The lattice based counting model however operates on a discrete spatial scale with each lattice box capturing the total effect in that box, and there it is theoretically permissible to have an independent "nugget effect", as it just leads to overdispersed now in the Poisson counts.

 The effect you're seeing in the estimates sound like the posterior simply says that there are parameter values for the spatial field that are better at capturing the structure than the nugget part of the model; the discretised spde model approximation error indeed tends to give slightly sharper correlation for short distances, so this wouldn't be surprising. In addition to that, the point process is extremely weakly informative about the small scale structure of the intensity process, so it's likely that the nugget effect has only a very small practical effect on the point pattern.  Unless your average count in each grid box is very high you won't be able to detect overdispersion.  And if you're working on a continuous domain, the nugget is nonsensical in the intensity process.

There may be other reasons for what you see, but the above are some basic modelling considerations.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLArs,

I am fitting a family of space-time models (one per year, for ten years) using inla.spde2.matern for the spatial component. The majority of the models behave well and seem to converge to similar values for the range and variance of the field. However, there are a couple of instances where the model misbehaves badly, and ends up in an extremely different configuration - essentially the spatial term ends up being extremely smooth, and the variability in the observations gets dumped into the observation error instead.

I would like to solve this problem by specifying a (relatively tight) prior that eliminates these undesirable solutions. In particular, I am looking at the parameters in inla.spde2.matern called "prior.variance.nominal" and "prior.range.nominal". However, as far as I see it, these arguments only set the mean of the priors on these parameters - how do I set the precision as well?

Best wishes,

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Use theta.prior.prec to specify the prior precisions. These are the precisions in the log-scale for the thetas. The interpretation depends on which parameterisation you use (via B.tau and B.kappa).  From your problem description it sounds like something like
theta.prior.prec=c(0.1, 1)
might help to suppress large range estimates. Unless you have replications of the model, this is often needed to disambiguate between spatial covariance and expectation.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

There are a number of packages that fit LGCPs.  (We only have one of them, so this information isn't complete.)

- The lgcp package fits LGCPs using a modern MCMC routine.

- The spatstat package fits LGCPs using non-Bayesian methods (the spatstat::lgcp.estK uses minimum contrast estimation)

- The geostatsp package provides a nice (and easy to use!) wrapper to the INLA package.

I hope this helps.

Dan

Morning,

  My name is Ara. I am PhD student at the University of New Mexico working on a global marine predator project. I was wondering if anyone has looked at how INLA behaves at different spatial scales. Currently I have a global grid at 880km2 and 110km2. We suspect that certain predictor variables will change as we change grid sizes but we are seeing some weirdness.

I am running R 3.2.4 (2016-03-10) and INLA 0.0.1455098891

ISSUE

messages.body_plain:
Hi Anna,

The problem with the Beasg (or ICAR(1)) model is that it doesn't behave consistently under refinement.  This means that you are comparing estimates from *very* different models!

There is also the issue that the model is ``unscaled'', which means that the ``precision parameter'' actually means quite different things between the models.  As the same priors are being used, this can lead to accidentally very informative priors.

For the first issue (Besag not behaving consistently under discretisation), I would recommend changing to SPDE priors.

For the second issue (i.e. if you want to stick with something like a Besag model), you can do some scaling.  The easiest version is to replace "model = "besag"" with "model = "bym2"".  This will also add an i.i.d. random effect in each cell.  If you'd rather turn it off and get the pure Besag model, you can use the following:

  f(idx, model = "bym2", graph = adj, hyper = list(phi=list(intial=15, fixed=TRUE) ) )

which fixes the mixing parameter phi to be approximately 1 (prior is on the logit scale), which corresponds to the Besag model.  Details can be found in this paper: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1601.01180.pdf

Fixing the scaling may be enough to fix the problem, but it may not be...

Hope this helps!

Dan

messages.subject_clean: About likelihood of log Gaussian Cox process
messages.body_plain:
Dear help,

I am using the SPDE model with INLA to fit a log Gaussian Cox process with marks - ref Simpson et al. 2016, Going off grid: computationally efficient inference for log-Gaussian Cox processes.
In the reference, the likelihood of a point pattern is given by
$$\pi(Y|\lambda) = \exp(|\Omega|-\int_{\Omega}\lambda(s) ds)\prod_{s_i\in Y}\lambda(s_i).$$
However, in some other references, such as "Bayesian geostatistical modelling with informative sampling locations" by Pati et al. (2011), the likelihood of such Poisson process is represented by
$$p(s_i)=\frac{\lambda(s_i)}{\int_{\Omega}\lambda(s) ds},$$
which is different from the one in Simpson et al. 2016..
I suppose the examples in the tutorial should use the one in Simpson et al. 2016, but may I ask what is the difference or connection between the two likelihoods?

Thanks a lot!
David Wang

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: About likelihood of log Gaussian Cox process
messages.body_plain:
Let's first define Lambda = int_Omega lambda(s) ds. Then
lambda(s) / Lambda
is the spatial density for each point in the point process, so it's _not_ a probability at
each location.

That said, implementing the likelihood
  ( prod_{i=1}^n lambda(s_i) ) / Lambda^n
actually looks harder than the Cox process likelihood (that includes the Poisson
probabilities for n, which cancels out Lambda^n), since the log-likelihood has the log of
the integral over Omega (the Cox process log-likelihood just has the integral itself).

I think something can be done in principle, but I'm not aware of it having been done in
R-INLA.  You may be better off treating it as a Cox process instead of treating n as a
fixed number.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

inla() uses multiple cores on shared memory systems by default.
You can control how many by setting the num.threads parameter (usually done only to limit the number of cores used, for large models that would use too much memory when running on all available cores).
It does not use clusters, since the implementation requires shared memory access via OpenMP only, and not MPI.

Finn
